extracted.intended_audience: inventors, product designers, entrepreneurs, and businesses considering or preparing U.S. ornamental (design) patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and legal guidance for determining eligibility, preparing, filing, and enforcing U.S. ornamental (design) patents, including substantive requirements, drawings/formalities, deadlines, and strategic IP considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornamental (non-functional) requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A design must be primarily decorative and not dictated by functional necessity; a design is ornamental if it is applied to an article of manufacture and is visible during normal use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted guidance from MPEP: ornamental means 'the appearance presented by the article which creates an impression through the eye upon the mind of the observer.' Courts use the functionality doctrine to deny design patents where claimed design is primarily dictated by function. Test whether alternative designs could achieve the same function — if no alternatives exist, the design is likely functional and not patentable as ornamental. Examples: a unique embossed pattern on a baby wipe qualifies; an ergonomically necessary curved wrench handle does not, whereas a wrench with intricate carvings purely for visual appeal may qualify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applied to an article of manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed design must be applied to an article of manufacture and the design must be an integral part of the item, not standalone artwork.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surface ornamentation alone can be protected only if part of an article. The design must be attached to or embodied in a manufacturable item (e.g., perfume bottle shape, fabric pattern on clothing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Visibility during normal use
rubrics_metrics.description: A design must be visible during normal use to qualify, although it can be primarily hidden and still qualify (examples: underwear lining, suitcase lining, inner sole of a shoe).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designs that are not observable during ordinary use may still qualify when displayed in a commercial setting or when visibility is reasonably expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty and non-obviousness over prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: No identical design can exist in prior art; the design must be novel and non-obvious over existing designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor differences are not enough. The USPTO searches existing ornamental design patents during examination; applicants should conduct thorough prior-art searches because even small similarities can disqualify a claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility and definiteness
rubrics_metrics.description: The design must be capable of being reproduced and must be definite, not the chance result of an existing method or random process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a randomly changing laser light pattern likely will not qualify, though the combined appearance of the light and the item on which it reflects might.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of protectable designs
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three major categories of ornamental design patents: shape and proportions; surface ornamentation; and a combination of shape/proportions and surface ornamentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: Apple iPhone (shape/proportions), decorative watch face (surface ornamentation), a new style of sneaker (combination).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on functional elements within claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Including design elements that serve a function (e.g., hinges, fasteners, ergonomically required contours) can compromise eligibility for a design patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you are trying to protect how something works, consider a utility patent instead. Courts and the USPTO will analyze whether claimed features are dictated by function rather than ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings and formality requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patent applications require very specific drawings: precise, black-and-white line drawings showing all views of the design (front, rear, top, bottom, both sides), and helpful three-dimensional views and exploded views for multiple components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The biggest portion of the application is the design patent drawings. Photos or poorly rendered images can lead to rejection. CAD renderings are acceptable only if they meet the USPTO’s strict requirements. Follow the USPTO design patent guide exactly; incorrect images often cause refusal or delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior-art search difficulty and counsel recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patents are harder to find through online databases because not all are published; therefore conducting a comprehensive search is important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work with a patent attorney who has access to more records and can conduct a thorough search and ensure drawings and other paperwork meet USPTO requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: 12-month U.S. filing deadline after public disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: After releasing the design publicly, you have 12 months to file a U.S. ornamental design patent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the design is kept secret, there is no timeline, but keeping it secret risks another party independently arriving at and filing for a similar design. Filing quickly after disclosure is crucial because delays can forfeit rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design patent term and maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: A U.S. design patent lasts 15 years from the date of grant and does not require maintenance fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term changed from 14 to 15 years in 2015 as a result of the Hague Agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement and infringement standard (ordinary observer)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove design patent infringement, the patent holder must show the ornamental features covered by the patent aren't present in prior art and that the accused product appropriates the protected design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis typically compares differences and similarities from the perspective of an ordinary observer to determine whether the accused design is substantially similar enough to cause confusion; courts consider whether the overall visual impression is appropriated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing process steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Core filing steps: review existing patents (prior art search); prepare documentation (especially drawings); file the design patent application; and wait for USPTO decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include front/rear/top/bottom/side views and 3D/exploded views as needed. If rejected, you can file a continued prosecution application to put your case in front of a different examiner. Typical review times are faster than utility patents (often 1–2 years, but could take up to 3 years).

rubrics_metrics.name: Common pitfalls causing delay or rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Common mistakes: inadequate or incorrect drawings, overlooking prior art, including functional claims, and waiting too long to file after public disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An experienced IP attorney can help avoid these avoidable errors and improve chances of approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic use within a broader IP strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patents are best used alongside other IP protections—utility patents for functions, trademarks (trade dress) for source-identifying shapes/packaging, and copyright for two-dimensional artwork.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Layered protection can enhance enforcement options and create additional remedies against look-alike products. Consider which forms of IP best match the aspects you want to protect.

rubrics_metrics.name: When not to use a design patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not pursue a design patent if the design is too similar to existing designs or if the claimed features are primarily functional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the design is not novel or is dictated by function, a design patent will likely be refused and pursuing it can expose you to infringement claims from existing patent holders. Evaluate alternatives (utility patent, trademark, copyright) and consult counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-patenting considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Some products may qualify for both utility and design patents, but there are restrictions that limit double-patenting the same item.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You must separately meet the requirements for each type of patent; there may be strategic and legal limitations on obtaining and enforcing both for the same product.
